title: Getting Started with Python AsyncIO
description: Learn how to use async/await in Python to build high-concurrency applications.
content:
# Introduction to AsyncIO

Asynchronous programming in Python allows your application to handle multiple I/O tasks (like network requests or file reads) without blocking the main execution thread.

## 1. Defining an Async Function

In modern Python (3.7+), async functions are declared using the `async def` syntax:

```python
import asyncio

async def fetch_data(task_id, delay):
    print(f"Task {task_id} starting...")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"Task {task_id} completed!")
    return f"Result {task_id}"

async def main():
    result = await fetch_data(1, 2)
    print(result)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

## 2. Running Tasks Concurrently

To run multiple async tasks simultaneously, use `asyncio.gather()`:

```python
async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_data(1, 2),
        fetch_data(2, 3),
        fetch_data(3, 1)
    )
    print("All tasks finished:", results)
```

## Summary
AsyncIO is ideal for I/O-bound operations such as web scraping, API calls, and chat applications.

content:
## Overview

C++ introduces modern stream I/O facilities (`<iostream>`) such as `std::cin` and `std::cout`, type-safe formatting, and flexible local variable declarations anywhere within a block.

## C++ Stream I/O Basics

The line #include `<iostream>` includes the declarations of the standard

stream Input/Output facilities as found in `<iostream>`. The std:: specifies that the name cout is in the standard-library namespace (we will discuss namespace on following blog, just forget it for now).

## Square and Cube Calculator

The following code demonstrates streams (`cin` and `cout`), user input, and formatted output:

```cpp
// input a number from user and get square and qube of it

#include <iostream>
using namespace std; //now we can use direct cout, cin etc without specify std::

int main()
{
     cout << "\nInput any number: "; // cout <<  is used to print
     int number; // we can define any datatype anywhere in a funtion
     cin >> number; // cin >>  is used to scan or get input

     int square = number * number;

     cout << "\nSquare of the number is " << square;
     cout << "\ncube of the number is " << number * number * number;

     return 0;
}
```

## C++ Style Headers

 In C, we used `<stdio.h>` header file. We can also use it in C++, but that looks old, so a new style header is presented by C++ that is `<iostream>`. Here is not .h extension to name iostream, it’s not specific reason but it is a new style header file so it is without .h, so just ignore it, as we can make any file without extension and include it in our code in both C or C++. ## Flexible Variable Declarations

 On the above code we see that in C++ we can declare local variables any where into a function code, but in C, we cannot do that; we must have to declare all the local variables on just starting of the function block in C.

## Comments in C++

```cpp
// This is the single-line comment

/*
This is an
example of
multi-line
comment in
C/C++.
*/
```

In the Visual Studio, we can use shortcuts for Line Comment: Ctrl + K, Ctrl + / Block Comment: Ctrl + Shift + / Comment selected line: Ctrl + K, Ctrl + C

Uncomment selected line: Ctrl + K, Ctrl + U

title: Introduction to C++
description: An introduction to C++, its origin under Bjarne Stroustrup, core OOP features, and why it remains in high demand.
content:
## Overview

C++ was invented by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1980 at Bell Labs as an extension of C with object-oriented constructs, initially dubbed "C with Classes".

## Core C++ Characteristics

- ** C++** was invented by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1980 at AT&T lab while adding Object-oriented constructs to the **C **language.
- **C++** is a General purpose OOP (Object –Oriented Programming) language.
- **C++** is a middle-level language, because it has both high and low level language features.
- ** C++** is a best programming language for computer hardware interaction, a lot of control hardware, memory management, better performance etc.
- ** C++** was initially called as “**C **with classes”, so we can say **C++** is an expanded version (new version) of C.
- Every **C **program can be compiled as **C++** but not every **C++** code is a **C **program.
- ** C++** supports both procedural and OOP concept, so it can also called as hybrid programming language.

## Object-Oriented Principles

C++ introduced the Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) paradigm to C, characterized by four primary pillars:

- I.   Abstraction
- II.  Encapsulation
- III. Polymorphism
- IV. Inheritance

We will discuss these terms on following blogs.

This is very short introduction, but just enough for remembering about “**C++** introduction”.

## Why C++?
- It is 40 years old and still high in demands.
- According to **Tiobe Index** of programming language,** C++** is ranked 4th in March 2020.
- ** C++** is most widely used programming language
- ** C++** is used in every fields of computer software like web, desktop app, mobile app etc.
- ** C++ **has been used to develop many famous projects like Facebook (social media), Amazon (web commerce), Google (web search) etc.
- ** C++ **has been used to develop many programming language like Java, JavaScript etc and web Browsers (e.g. Internet explorer, Mozilla Firefox, Safari, Chrome etc.)
- ** C++** is also used in to create graphics,  games, program system’s hardware.

There may be more other many applications of **C++ **that we have missed here, but these are enough to make it more interesting.

On next following blog we direct start with code samples to understand it. Hopefully it may be very helpful in learning **C++**

title: Pointers
description: Introduction to C pointers, memory addresses, the & and * operators, pointer base types, and pointer assignments.
content:
## Overview

A **pointer** is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Pointers are one of C's most powerful features, enabling dynamic memory allocation, efficient array passing, and low-level hardware access.

For example, if one variable contains the address of another variable, the first variable is said to “pointer to the second”.

Suppose second variable is an **int** type then the first variable's type is called “pointer to integer” (int*)

## Why Pointers Are Used

1) Pointers can be used in functions so that their calling arguments could be modified

2) Pointers support dynamic memory allocation.

3) Pointers can improve the efficiency of certain routines().

4) Pointers provide support for dynamic data structures, such as binary trees and linked lists.

## Safe Pointer Practices

Pointers are one of the strongest but also one of the most dangerous features in C/C++.

For example, a pointer containing an invalid value can cause a program to crash.

Using pointers incorrectly, causing bugs that are very difficult to find.

## Declaring Pointer Variables

A pointer must be declared before we use it. A pointer declaration consists of a base type, an *, and the variable name. The general form for declaring a pointer variable is

type *name;

where type is the base type of the pointer and may be any valid type. The name of the pointer variable is specified by name.

1) The base type of the pointer defines the type of object to which the pointer will point.

2) any type of pointer can point anywhere in memory.

3) all pointer operations are done relative to the pointer's base type.

(an int * pointer always "thinks" that it points to an int object, no matter what that piece of memory actually contains.)

## The Pointer Operators (& and *)

There are two pointer operators: * and &.

The & is a unary operator that returns the memory address of its operand & called as reference operator. (Or we speak it **ampersand**)

m = &count;

places into m the memory address of the variable count.

This address is the computer's internal location of the variable. It has nothing to do with the value of count. We can think of **&** as "the address of." Therefore,  m=**&**count means "m receives the address of count".

for example: if the variable count uses memory location 2000 to store its value, Also suppose that count has a value of 100. Then, m=&count means, m will have the value 2000.

pointer operator, *, is the complement of &.

It is a unary operator that returns the value located at the address that follows. For example, if m contains the memory address of the variable count,

q = *m;

assigns the value of count into q. Thus, q will have the value 100 because 100 is stored at location 2000, which is the memory address that was stored in m. we can think of * as "at address." In this case, the preceding statement can be said as "q receives the value at address m".

## Pointer Expressions & Base Types

**i) ****Pointer Assignments:**

We can use a pointer on the right-hand side of an assignment statement to assign its value to another pointer, when both pointers are the same type.

Example:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
     int x = 99;
     int *p1, *p2;
     p1 = &x;  p2 = p1;
     printf("Values at p1 and p2: %d % d\n", *p1, *p2);  /* print the value of x twice */
     printf("Addresses pointed to by p1 and p2: %p %p", p1, p2); /* print the address of x twice */

     getchar();
     return 0;
}
```

After the assignment sequence

p1 = &x; p2 = p1;

p1 and p2 both point to x. Thus, both p1 and p2 refer to the same object.

The addresses are displayed by using the %p format specifier.

**ii) ****Pointer Conversions:**

A pointer can be converted into another type of pointer. There are two categories of this conversion:

**1)** involve void* pointers, and

**2)** explicit cast (don't include void*)

it is permissible to assign a void* pointer to any other type of pointer.

It is also permissible to assign any other type of pointer to a void* pointer.

A void* pointer is called a **generic pointer**.

The void* pointer is used to specify a pointer whose base type is unknown.

Except for void*, all other pointer conversions must be performed by using an explicit cast. It may be happen that the conversion of one type of pointer into another type can make undefined behavior.

For example, checkout the following program:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
     float x = 100.1, y;  int *p;
     /* below statement causes p (which is an integer pointer) to point to a float. */
     p = (int *)&x;
     /* below statement does not operate as expected. */
     y = *p;    /* attempt to assign y the value x through p */
                      /* The following statement will not output 100.1. */
     printf("The(incorrect) value of x is : %f", y);
     getchar();
     return 0;
}
```

content: ## Overview A statement in C is a syntactic command executed sequentially by the processor. Statements fall into five major categories. ## 1. Selection Statements Also called as conditional statements. For example- **if – else**, **? Operator **and **switch** ## 2. Iteration (Loop) Statements Iteration statements (also called loops) allow a set of expressions to be executed repeatedly until a condition is reached. This condition may be predetermined (as in the **for** loop) or open ended (as in the **while** and **do**-**while** loops). For example- **for**, **while**, **do-while **loops ## 3. Jump Statements This statement transfers control flow. For example- **goto**, **break**, **continue**, **return ** ## 4. Label Statements For example- identifier followed by a colon ( **: **) ## 5. Expression & Block Statements An expression is followed by a semicolon (**;**) For example- printf("statement 1"); 6) Block A group of expressions in **{ } **is called as block. For example- { printf("statement 1"); printf("statement 2"); printf("statement 3") ;}

content:
## Overview

Operators are symbols that instruct the compiler to perform specific mathematical, relational, or logical manipulations on operands.

## Arithmetic Operators

| Operator Name | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Basic assignment | a = b |
| Addition | a + b |
| Subtraction | a - b |
| Unary plus | +a |
| Unary minus | -a |
| Multiplication | a * b |
| Division | a / b |
| Modulo (integer remainder) | a % b |
| Increment (Prefix) | ++a |
| Increment (Postfix) | a++ |
| Decrement (Prefix) | ++a |
| Decrement (Postfix) | a++ |

## Comparison & Relational Operators

| Operator Name | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Equal to | a == b |
| Not equal to | a != b |
| Greater than | a > b |
| Less than | a < b |
| Greater than or equal to | a >= b |
| Less than or equal to | a <= b |

## Logical Operators

| Operator Name | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Logical negation (NOT) | !a |
| Logical AND | a && b |
| Logical OR | a \|\| b |

## Bitwise Operators

| Operator Name | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Bitwise NOT | ~a |
| Bitwise AND | a & b |
| Bitwise OR | a \| b |
| Bitwise XOR | a ^ b |
| Bitwise left shift | a << b |
| Bitwise right shift | a >> b |

**Compound assignment operators:**

| Operator Name | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Addition assignment | a += b |
| Subtraction assignment | a -= b |
| Multiplication assignment | a *= b |
| Division assignment | a /= b |
| Modulo assignment | a %= b |
| Bitwise AND assignment | a &= b |
| Bitwise OR assignment | a \|= b |
| Bitwise XOR assignment | a ^= b |
| Bitwise left shift assignment | a <<= b |
| Bitwise right shift assignment | a >>= b |

**Member and pointer operators:**

| Subscript | a[b] |
| Indirection("object pointed to by a") | *a |
| Address-of ("address of a") | &a |

## Other & Special Operators

title: Type Qualifiers
description: Understand C type qualifiers (const, volatile, restrict) and how they modify variable mutability and compiler optimizations.
content:
## Overview

Type qualifiers in C modify the behavior and accessibility of data types, informing the compiler about mutability, caching, and aliasing properties.

For example before **int, **if we add **const **(a type qualifier) the type **const int **will represent a constant integer datatype. And so an object defined with type **const int** can only initialized but may not be changed throughout the program.

Type qualifiers is used to controls the variable in a manner that how it is accessed or modified.

Type qualifiers have 3 types:

## 1. The const Qualifier

## 2. The volatile Qualifier

## 3. The restrict Qualifier

[Note: third one (**restrict**) is available in only c99 and above compiler versions.]

**const:**

As before discussed variable of **const type **may not be changed throughout the program. These variable stored in Read Only Memory. Also we must initialize with the definition.

For example:

**const float** pi = 3.1415; is OK

but we cannot write

| const float pi; pi = 3.1415; |
| :--- |

is wrong because pi is redefined here. When we declare a variable it automatically assigned with some garbage value.

More examples:

const char exp = ‘E’;

const int ten = 10;

etc.

**volatile:**

This qualifier indicates that the value of a variable of **volatile type** may be changed between different accesses, even if it is not modified in the program.

or

A **volatile type** variable’s value may be changed in a way not explicitly specified by the program.

For example, if 0x56 is assumed to be the value of a port that can be changed by external conditions only, then below declaration would prevent any possibility of accidental side effects:

**const volatile char** *port = (**const volatile char** *)  0x56;

**restrict:**

restrict keyword basically used with pointers declaration.

restrict keyword says to compiler that only the pointer itself or a value directly derived from it, will be used to access the object to which it points*.*

title: Variable Initialization and Constants
description: Learn how global, static, and local variables are initialized in C, alongside hexadecimal, octal, and string constants.
content: ## Overview Variables in C can be initialized during declaration. Constants are fixed values that cannot be altered during program execution. ## Variable Initialization Rules Global and static local variables are initialized only at the start of program. Local variables (excluding static local variables) are initialized each time in the block in which they are declared. If a local variable is not initialized or assigned to a value (constant), it will have unknown value. global and static local variables that are not initialized automatically set to zero or null value. ## Constants in C Sometimes also called as **literals. Constant** can be a value of any basic data type. For example: Integer constants – any integer number, e.g. 0, 1, 5, 17,30 etc. Float constant- any fractional number, e.g. 12.235, 3.141529, 2.714, 3.14e-10 etc. [Note: C also allows to use scientific notation for floating-point constants.] Character constant – any single character (excluding Backslash Character) enclosed in single quotes, e.g. ‘a’,’4’, ‘%’ etc. [Note: To get a Backslash Character we use double Backslash in single quotes e.g. ‘\\’. See **escape sequences.**] For assigning a character variable to null character, we use either ‘\0’ or simply 0. e.g. char x = ‘\0’; or char x = 0; For assigning a character variable to backslash character we use ‘\\’. e.g. char x = ‘\\’; Compiler optimizes a numeric constant into the smallest compatible data type that can hold it. For example: If integer is of 16 bit, 34 is int by default, but 23453453 is a long int, even though the value 34 could fit into a character type, the compiler will not cross type boundaries (excluding in the case of floating point constants where a float constant is assumed to be doubles). We can use a suffix to specify a constant precisely, see below list. | Data Type | Constants | | :--- | :--- | | int | 2, -4, 345 etc. | | long int | 2L, -4L, 3456789L, 67l, -41l etc. | | long long | 323434LL, 5657567ll, -5656ll etc. | | unsigned int | 2U, 4U, 876U, 7u, 768u etc. | | unsigned long long | 18446744073709551615ULL, 546ull etc. | | float | 34.34456F, -3.14256f, 2.6e-10f etc. | | double | 3.0,234.50, -9.765544545 etc. | | long double | 112324.45L,34534534645.455l etc. | ## Hexadecimal and Octal Constants An octal constant begins with a 0 and hexadecimal constant begins with 0x, for example: | int octa = 0123; | /* 83 in decimal */ | | :--- | :--- | | int hexa = 0x123; | /* 291 in decimal */ | [Note: In GNU GCC compiler, we can also use 0b or 0B for binary constants.] ## String Constants string is a set of characters enclosed in double quotes. For example: “this is a string”, “a”, “1234”, “3.1415926”, “#$a12” etc. [Note: **C** does not have a basic datatype of string but we can define string constant. To store the value of string constant into a string variable, we require a character array or character pointer. See arrays and pointers.] [Note: 'a' and “a” both are different here. 'a' is a character constant while “a” is a string constant.] **Escape Sequences: ** Escape sequences is used by using backslash character. Sometimes also called as **Backslash Character Constants.** Below is a list with the backslash character constant and its meaning. | B.C.C. | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | \b | Backspace | | \f | Form feed | | \n | New line | | \r | Carriage return | | \t | Horizontal tab | | \" | Double quote | | \` | Single quote | | \ \ | Backslash | | \v | Vertical tab | | \a | Alert | | \? | Question mark | | \N | Octal constant (where N is an octal constant) | | \xN | Hexadecimal constant (where N is a hexadecimal constant) | Escape sequences is mostly used in string constants or printing in desired pattern.

title: Learning C
description: Learn the foundational building blocks of C, from the character set (alphabets, digits, symbols) to tokens and instructions.
content:
## Overview

Learning C is structured like learning a natural language:

1. In English, we start with **alphabets**, combine alphabets to construct **words**, assemble words into **sentences**, and organize sentences into **paragraphs**.
2. In C, we start with the **character set** (alphabets, digits, and special symbols), combine them into **tokens** (constants, variables, and keywords), assemble tokens into **instructions**, and organize instructions into a complete **program**.

## C Character Set

The table below lists the valid alphabets, numbers, and special symbols recognized by standard C compilers:

| Category | Allowed Characters |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Alphabets** | `A-Z`, `a-z` |
| **Digits** | `0-9` |
| **Special Symbols** | `~ ' ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) _ - + = | \ { } [ ] : ; " ' < > , . ? /` |

## Language Building Blocks

- **Character Set**: Foundational alphabets, digits, and symbols.
- **Constants, Variables & Keywords**: Named tokens holding values or reserving compiler actions.
- **Instructions / Statements**: Syntactic units that perform arithmetic, assignments, or control flow.
- **Program**: A collection of functions and instructions executed by the operating system.

title: C, C99, ANSI C and GNU C
description: Understand the evolution of C standards, from K&R C and ANSI C (C89/C90) to C99, C11, and GNU C extensions.
content:
## Overview

Since its creation in 1972, the C programming language has evolved through several standardized revisions, from early K&R C to ANSI C (C89/C90), C99, C11, and modern extensions supported by GCC (GNU C).

## The Evolution of C Standards

1. **K&R C**: The original informal specification described in Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie's 1978 book *The C Programming Language*.
2. **ANSI C / ISO C (C89 / C90)**: Standardized in 1989/1990, establishing function prototypes, standard library headers, and portability guarantees.
3. **C99**: Introduced variable declarations anywhere in block scope, `//` single-line comments, `inline` functions, flexible array members, and boolean types (`<stdbool.h>`).
4. **GNU C**: GCC extensions providing compiler attributes (`__attribute__`), inline assembly, and statement expressions.

## Comparison of C Versions

## References & Further Reading

[https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17206568/what-is-the-difference-between-c-c99-ansi-c-and-gnu-c](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17206568/what-is-the-difference-between-c-c99-ansi-c-and-gnu-c)

| “Everything before standardization is generally called "K&R C", after the famous book, with Dennis Ritchie, the inventor of the C language, as one of the authors. This was "the C language" from 1972-1989. The first C standard was released 1989 nationally in USA, by their national standard institute ANSI. This release is called C89 or ANSI-C. From 1989-1990 this was "the C language". The year after, the American standard was accepted internationally and published by ISO (ISO 9899:1990). This release is called C90. Technically, it is the same standard as C89/ANSI-C. Formally, it replaced C89/ANSI-C, making them obsolete. From 1990-1999, C90 was "the C language". Please note that since 1989, ANSI haven't had anything to do with the C language. Programmers still speaking about "ANSI C" generally haven't got a clue about what it means. ISO "owns" the C language, through the standard ISO 9899. A minor update was released in 1995, sometimes referred to as "C95". This was not a major revision, but rather a technical amendment formally named ISO/IEC 899:1990/Amd.1:1995. The main change was introduction of wide character support. In 1999, the C standard went through a major revision (ISO 9899:1999). This version of the standard is called C99. From 1999-2011, this was "the C language". In 2011, the C standard was changed again (ISO 9899:2011). This version is called C11. Various new features like _Generic, _Static_assert and thread support were added to the language. The update had a lot of focus on multi-core, multi-processing and expression sequencing. From 2011-2017, this was "the C language". In 2017, C11 was revised and various defect reports were solved. This standard is informally called C17 and was released as ISO 9899:2018. It contains no new features, just corrections. It is the current version of the C language. "C99 strict" likely refers to a compiler setting forcing a compiler to follow the standard by the letter. There is a term conforming implementation in the C standard. Essentially it means: "this compiler actually implements the C language correctly". Programs that implement the C language correctly are formally called strictly conforming programs. "GNU C" can mean two things. Either the C compiler itself that comes as part of the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC). Or it can mean the non-standard default setup that the GCC C compiler uses. If you compile with gcc program.c then you don't compile according to the C standard, but rather a non-standard GNU setup, which may be referred to as "GNU C". For example, the whole Linux kernel is made in non-standard GNU C, and not in standard C. If you want to compile your programs according to the C standard, you should type gcc -std=c99 -pedantic-errors. Replace c99 with c11 if your GCC version supports it. ” |
| :--- |

title: Introduction to C programming
description: Discover the origins, compilation pipeline, keywords, and foundational 'Hello World' structure of the C programming language.
content:
## Overview

C is a general-purpose programming language developed at AT&T's Bell Laboratories in 1972 by Dennis Ritchie on a DEC PDP-11 minicomputer running UNIX.

C is widely considered a middle-level language because it combines the power, structured logic, and clarity of high-level languages with the low-level memory addressing and hardware control of assembly language. It serves as the bedrock for modern operating systems, virtual machines, database engines, and runtime systems.

## How C Works: The Compilation Pipeline

C source code undergoes a multi-stage compilation process before execution:

1. **Source Code (`.c`)**: Human-readable source text written by the developer.
2. **Preprocessor**: Processes directives like `#include` and `#define`.
3. **Compiler**: Translates C code into assembly or native machine object files (`.obj` / `.o`).
4. **Linker**: Combines object files with standard C runtime libraries into an executable binary (`.exe` / ELF).

> **Compiler vs. Interpreter**: Unlike an interpreter (which executes instructions line by line), a C compiler processes the whole program ahead of time, producing high-performance machine code.

## Reserved C Keywords

Keywords are predefined reserved words that possess special syntactic meanings to the C compiler and cannot be used as user-defined variable or function names:

| Group A–D | Group E–I | Group L–S | Group S–W |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `auto` | `else` | `long` | `sizeof` |
| `break` | `enum` | `register` | `static` |
| `case` | `extern` | `return` | `struct` |
| `char` | `float` | `short` | `switch` |
| `const` | `for` | `signed` | `typedef` |
| `continue` | `goto` | | `union` |
| `default` | `if` | | `unsigned` |
| `do` | `int` | | `void` |
| `double` | | | `volatile` / `while` |

## Hello World in C

```c
// A "Hello World" program using C language
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("hello world\n");

    getchar();
    return 0;
}
```

## Code Explanation

- `#include <stdio.h>`: Preprocessor directive including the Standard Input/Output library header containing prototypes for `printf()` and `getchar()`.
- `int main(void)`: Defines the primary entry point where execution begins.
- `printf("hello world\n")`: Emits the formatted string to the console stdout.
- `return 0`: Conveys exit status code '0' to the operating system, confirming successful program termination.
